Ice Bucket Challenge
EYES BUK-it CHAL-inj
noun (Millennial slang)
A 2014 viral campaign in which participants filmed themselves dumping a bucket of ice water over their heads, nominated others to do the same within twenty-four hours, and donated to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) research. It was popularized in July–August 2014 by Pete Frates, a former Boston College baseball captain with ALS, and Pat Quinn of New York, who also had the disease. More than seventeen million videos were posted and the ALS Association received about $115 million. Some Christian leaders cautioned that the Association funded embryonic stem-cell research and directed gifts to other ALS charities.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Ice Bucket Challenge was the great viral charity event of 2014: film yourself getting soaked with ice water, nominate three friends, and donate to fight ALS. Celebrities, athletes, politicians, and millions of ordinary people joined. The Christian observation has more than one side. On the good side, real money went to research for a cruel disease, and men who were dying, Pete Frates and Pat Quinn, saw their friends rally around them. Scripture commends generosity: "He which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully … for God loveth a cheerful giver" (2Co 9:6-7). On the side that deserves examination: first, the challenge mixed giving with self-display, filmed and posted, when the Lord Jesus said, "when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret" (Mat 6:3-4). Many took the challenge and never gave at all. Second, the ethics of where the money went mattered. Some Christians noted that the beneficiary funded research on human embryos, and directed their gifts to ALS charities that respect the life of the unborn. That was not killjoy; it was obedience to the sixth commandment and to the truth that God forms life in the womb (Psa 139:13). A father teaches his children to give generously, to give mostly in secret, and to ask where their gifts go, so that compassion for one suffering person is never paid for with the lives of the smallest.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial viral charity campaign (summer 2014) for ALS: ice water, nominations, donations; real generosity (2Co 9:7) mixed with public display (Mat 6:3-4), with a Christian caution about embryonic research funding (Psa 139:13).

ICE BUCKET CHALLENGE, n. (Millennial viral campaign, 2014) A filmed challenge to pour ice water over one’s head, nominate others, and donate to ALS research. Raised about $115 million for the ALS Association.

Webster (1828), root challenge: CHALLENGE, noun Literally, a calling, or crying out, the primary sense of many words expressing a demand, as claim. Hence appropriately, 1. A calling upon one to fight in single combat; an invitation or summons, verbal or written, to decide a controversy by a duel. Hence the letter containing the summons is also called a challenge 2. A claim or demand made of a right or supposed right. There must be no challenge of superiority. 3. Among hunters, the opening and crying of hounds at the first finding the scent of their game. […]

Decode for parents: teach your children to give generously, quietly, and wisely, asking where their gifts go.

Key Scripture

2Co 9:7 — "Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."

Mat 6:3-4 — "But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly."

Psa 139:13 — "For thou hast possessed my reins: thou hast covered me in my mother's womb."

Gal 6:10 — "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith."

Pro 3:27 — "Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it."

Modern Corruption

The Ice Bucket Challenge joined real generosity to public display and, for some, to morally troubling research; Scripture asks for cheerful, secret, and conscientious giving.

expand to see more

The corruption is the merger of charity and performance. The challenge’s genius was that it made giving shareable; its weakness was that sharing could replace giving. The video became the point, the donation optional. A culture of "awareness" can feel virtuous while doing little. And generosity without discernment can fund wrong things: compassion for the sick must never be purchased with the destruction of human embryos, who are lives formed by God.

The redemption is generous, wise, and humble giving. "Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it" (Pro 3:27). Christians should be the first to help the sick, including those with ALS, and the most careful about how. Teach the young to give from their own money, to do much of it in secret, to research charities, and to love the suffering neighbour in ways that honour every human life.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French chalenge (accusation, claim) → challenge (a call to contest) → 2014 Ice Bucket Challenge (Frates, Quinn) → viral-charity template.
